summary: Psalm 140 is a plea for rescue from violent and deceptive enemies. The speaker describes plots, poisonous speech, snares, and traps, then turns to Yahweh as God, protector, and judge. The psalm ends in confidence that Yahweh will uphold the afflicted and that the upright will live in his presence.
whyItMatters: This chapter shows how the Psalms give words for danger without pretending the danger is small. It also places a hard prayer for judgment inside an appeal to God rather than an act of personal revenge.

context.author: The heading says, “A Psalm by David,” but such headings may indicate authorship, association, dedication, or belonging; readers differ on how much the heading establishes.
context.audience: Israel’s worshiping and instructed community, with later Jewish and Christian communities also adopting the Psalms for public prayer and private life.
context.date: The Psalms are an anthology formed over time; individual poems may preserve material from the monarchy through the postexilic period, so one fixed date for Psalm 140 should not be claimed from this chapter alone.
context.setting: Book V of Psalms, where prayers, thanksgiving, Torah reflection, pilgrimage songs, and praise stand together in the final movement of the Psalter.
context.literaryForm: Hebrew poetic prayer of distress, using vivid images, repeated petitions, and confidence in God’s justice.

outline.heading: A plea for protection
outline.note: The speaker asks Yahweh for deliverance from evil and violent men, describing their plans for war and their speech as venomous.

outline.heading: Hidden traps
outline.note: The prayer repeats the request for preservation and names the danger as snares, nets, cords, and traps set along the path.

outline.heading: Trust in Yahweh
outline.note: The speaker addresses Yahweh as “my God” and remembers him as the strength of salvation and protection in battle.

outline.heading: A prayer against the wicked
outline.note: The speaker asks that the wicked not succeed and that their own mischief and destructive plans return on them.

outline.heading: Confidence in justice
outline.note: The psalm closes by declaring that evil speech and violence will not finally stand, while Yahweh maintains the cause of the afflicted and the upright dwell in his presence.

keyVerses.text: For the Chief Musician. A Psalm by David. Deliver me, Yahweh, from evil men. Preserve me from violent men:
keyVerses.why: The opening gives the chapter its basic cry: the speaker is threatened and asks Yahweh for deliverance and preservation.

keyVerses.text: I said to Yahweh, “You are my God.” Listen to the cry of my petitions, Yahweh.
keyVerses.why: This verse shows that the prayer is not only complaint; it is spoken from personal trust in Yahweh.

keyVerses.text: Yahweh, don’t grant the desires of the wicked. Don’t let their evil plans succeed, or they will become proud. Selah.
keyVerses.why: The request focuses on stopping evil plans before they succeed and strengthen the proud.

keyVerses.text: I know that Yahweh will maintain the cause of the afflicted, and justice for the needy.
keyVerses.why: This line anchors the psalm’s final confidence: Yahweh is expected to uphold the vulnerable and act justly.

themes: justice for the afflicted and needy

questions.question: Who is speaking in this psalm?
questions.answer: The heading identifies the psalm as “A Psalm by David.” Readers differ on whether such headings function as direct authorship, association with David, dedication, or collection marking. The poem itself speaks in the first person as someone threatened by evil and violent men.

questions.question: What kind of danger does the speaker describe?
questions.answer: The danger includes violent people, planned mischief, warlike gathering, poisonous speech, and hidden traps. The chapter does not give a narrative setting or name the enemies. It presents the threat through images rather than a case history.

questions.question: What does “Selah” mean here?
questions.answer: “Selah” appears after verses 3, 5, and 8. It is a musical or performance marker whose exact instruction is uncertain. It appears after descriptions of venomous speech, traps, and the request that evil plans fail.

questions.question: Why does the psalm compare speech to a serpent and viper’s poison?
questions.answer: The image says that the enemies’ tongues are sharpened and their lips carry poison. The point is not zoology but the harm done by speech. In this chapter, words are part of violence because they devise, accuse, and threaten.

questions.question: Is the speaker asking for personal revenge?
questions.answer: The speaker asks Yahweh to act, not claiming to carry out punishment himself. Verses 8-10 ask that evil plans fail and that destructive speech and violence turn back on those who use them. Readers differ on how to pray such lines today, but the chapter itself places the cry for judgment before Yahweh.

questions.question: Why are verses 9-10 so severe?
questions.answer: They ask for the surrounding enemies’ own mischief to cover them and for burning coals, fire, and miry pits to overtake them. The language is morally intense and should not be flattened into a mild wish. Within the psalm, it expresses the plea that violent schemes not be allowed to triumph.

questions.question: What changes when the speaker says, “You are my God”?
questions.answer: The danger has not disappeared, but the address becomes more direct and trusting. The speaker moves from describing enemies to naming Yahweh as God and asking him to listen. Verse 7 then remembers Yahweh as the strength of salvation and protection in battle.

questions.question: Who are “the afflicted” and “the needy” in verse 12?
questions.answer: The psalm does not identify them by name. In context, they are people whose cause needs to be maintained and who need justice against violent and wicked people. The speaker includes himself among those depending on Yahweh’s defense.

questions.question: How does the psalm end after so much danger?
questions.answer: It ends with confidence rather than a report that the enemies have already vanished. The righteous give thanks to Yahweh’s name, and the upright dwell in his presence. The closing trusts Yahweh’s justice even while the prayer itself began in distress.

glossary.def: A phrase in the heading that signals a performance or worship setting, though the exact ancient role is not explained in the chapter.
A preserved performance marker in the psalm; its exact instruction is uncertain, so its appearance does not establish a precise performance instruction.
Harmful plotting or troublemaking; in this chapter the enemies devise it in their hearts, and the speaker asks that the harm of their own words return on them.
A trap image used for the danger hidden by the proud along the speaker’s path.
